summary: Proposes an ACME extension for issuing a sequence of short-lived certificates that are renewed automatically. Because each certificate expires quickly, a compromised key can be dealt with by simply stopping renewal, instead of relying on revocation, which is often unreliable.

eli5.summary: Instead of one long-lasting ID card you must hunt down if stolen, you get a new one that expires quickly each day. If it goes missing, you just stop getting new ones.

questions: how do short-lived certificates replace revocation
how do you cancel a star certificate order
subtitle: An ACME extension where the CA keeps reissuing short-lived certificates, so a compromised key is handled by stopping renewal instead of revoking.

tldr.problem: Revoking a certificate after its private key is exposed is often unreliable. Getting a string of short-lived certificates through plain ACME would mean repeating the whole ACME process every few days.
tldr.mechanism: The client places one ACME Order with an auto-renewal object. The CA then reissues the certificate from the same CSR before each one expires and publishes it at a fixed star-certificate URL until the Order is canceled or reaches its end date.
tldr.outcome: Expiry replaces revocation: the identifier owner cancels the Order and the last certificate lapses shortly after. The trade-off is that cancellation is not instant, since the next certificate may already be published.

facts.label: Next certificate published
facts.value: At the latest halfway through the current lifetime

facts.label: Recommended Web lifetime
facts.value: No longer than 4 days (excluding clock-skew adjustment)

today: RFC 8739 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2020. The metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on ACME as defined in RFC 8555.

sections.title: Why Short-Term Certificates
sections.content:
The ACME protocol (RFC 8555) automates issuing a certificate to a named entity, called the Identifier Owner (IdO). The identifier is usually a domain name. If the IdO wants a string of short-term certificates from the same private key, for example one every 2-3 days, it would have to go through the whole ACME protocol each time. That makes issuance heavily dependent on both the CA and the identity infrastructure, such as DNS and web servers.

RFC 8739 makes short-term certificates first-class objects in ACME. Once the Order is accepted, the CA is responsible for publishing the next certificate at an agreed URL before the previous one expires. The IdO can stop the renewal early, for example on key compromise.

One named use case is name delegation between a CDN or cloud provider and its customers: the customer ends the delegation by telling the CA to stop renewing and letting the active certificate expire.
sections.eli5: Asking for a fresh pass every few days is tiring. This lets the office keep handing you a new pass automatically until you say stop.

sections.title: The Three Phases
sections.content:
The protocol has three phases.

  • Bootstrap: the IdO, acting as an ACME client, asks for a certificate with a short validity (for example 24 to 72 hours, depending on the use case), automatic renewal for a set period, and a highly available download location. It still completes the usual ACME challenges. The phase ends when the CA adds the STAR certificate URL to the Order.
  • Auto-renewal: the CA reissues the certificate using the same CSR, so the same identifier and public key, before the old one expires, and publishes it at that URL. The user of the certificate may be the IdO or a delegated third party.
  • Termination: the IdO sends a cancellation to the Order. The CA stops renewal, makes the publication resource return an error, and sets the Order status to canceled.

It is not necessary to explicitly revoke the short-term certificate.
sections.eli5: First you sign up, then the office mails you fresh passes by itself, and at the end you can cancel the subscription.

sections.title: Order and Directory Extensions
sections.content:
The Order resource gains an auto-renewal object that MUST be present for STAR certificates. Its fields are start-date (optional), end-date (required), lifetime (required, seconds, the maximum validity of each certificate), lifetime-adjust (optional, seconds of left padding, default 0) and allow-certificate-get (optional). The notBefore and notAfter fields from RFC 8555 MUST NOT appear in a STAR Order, or the server returns 400 with type malformedRequest. The Order also gets a star-certificate URL in place of certificate, and a new status value canceled. The status stays valid while certificates are being issued.

To cancel, the client POSTs {status: canceled} to the Order URL. After that the server MUST NOT issue more certificates, and it MUST respond with 403 to requests to the star-certificate endpoint. Canceling an Order that is not valid yields a 400 with type autoRenewalCancellationInvalid. Explicit revocation of a STAR certificate is not supported: the server MUST return 403 with type autoRenewalRevocationNotSupported.

Servers advertise support through an auto-renewal object in the directory meta field, with min-lifetime, max-duration and optionally allow-certificate-get.
sections.eli5: The sign-up form gets new boxes: when to start, when to stop, and how long each pass lasts. The office also publishes the shortest pass length it allows.

sections.title: Fetching the Certificates
sections.content:
Normally the certificate is fetched from the star-certificate endpoint with POST-as-GET. If both sides negotiate it, the client may use a plain unauthenticated GET instead. The server advertises this with allow-certificate-get in the directory, the client asks for it per Order, and the server MUST still accept POST-as-GET. This helps name delegation, since the delegated party does not hold the ACME account key, and it lets HTTP caches help. With unauthenticated GET the server SHALL set cache directives so caches treat the response as stale by the time the certificate expires.

The server SHOULD send Cert-Not-Before and Cert-Not-After headers, which MUST equal the dates in the end-entity certificate. They let clients that do not parse certificates know the validity window.

The next certificate MUST be published at the latest halfway through the lifetime of the current one, and its notBefore MUST already have passed at publication. Because of this, a cancellation is not fully effective until that next certificate also expires. For an expired Order the server MUST answer 403, ideally with type autoRenewalExpired.
sections.eli5: You can pick up your pass at a public window without showing your membership card, as long as the office agreed. A fresh pass is always on the shelf before the old one runs out.

sections.title: Computing Validity Dates
sections.content:
The nominal renewal date nrd[i] is when the i-th certificate is due. Dates step forward by the Order's lifetime T, starting with the first certificate and bounded by end-date. The validity of the i-th certificate is:

  • notAfter = min(nrd[i] + T, end)
  • notBefore = nrd[i] - max(adjust_client, adjust_server)

Here adjust_client is the smaller of T and the client's lifetime-adjust, and adjust_server is f * T, where f is at least .5 and less than 1, to ensure a published certificate is already valid. The server MUST NOT set the first certificate's notBefore before the start date.

In the RFC's example, a 4-day lifetime with a 3-day adjust gives three certificates between 2019-01-10 and 2019-01-20.
sections.eli5: Each pass is stamped to start a little early and end on schedule, so overlapping passes mean you are never caught without a valid one.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
What counts as short term is relative. In practice the lifetime will be counted in minutes, hours or days. Clients with wrong clocks cause many browser HTTPS errors, so site owners can use lifetime-adjust to backdate notBefore. The RFC cites 5 days covering 97.3% and 7 days covering 99.6% of the clock-skewed population.

A STAR certificate and a certificate with the OCSP must-staple flag are considered roughly equivalent when lifetimes match. Because OCSP responses can be cached for about 4 days on average, a STAR certificate used on the Web is RECOMMENDED to have an effective lifetime of no more than 4 days, not counting clock-skew adjustment.

For Certificate Transparency logs, the RFC reports that existing implementations could sustain the roughly 100-fold higher ingestion rate if STAR became the only issuance model. For caching, authenticated POST-as-GET cannot easily be cached, which makes clients more dependent on the ACME server, so unauthenticated GET is suggested to reduce that risk.
sections.eli5: If your watch is wrong you might think a pass is not valid yet. Starting passes a bit early keeps those people from being turned away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No revocation. STAR gives up the ability to revoke; expiry replaces it, so there may be a delay. The RFC points out that CRLs and OCSP responses have nextUpdate fields typically set hours, days or weeks ahead, so revocation has timeliness limits too. One special risk: if an Order has a start date well in the future and an attacker gets the private key and the first, post-dated certificate, cancellation will not help. IdOs are therefore RECOMMENDED to place Orders close to the start date.

Denial of service. One Order can produce dozens or hundreds of certificates, and an attacker could choose a tiny lifetime such as 1 second. CAs SHOULD enforce a minimum lifetime or rate limit internal issuance, counting renewals already scheduled.

Privacy. With unauthenticated GET, servers SHOULD choose non-guessable certificate URLs, for example capability URLs, to avoid correlating certificates by account.
sections.eli5: Stopping the subscription does not recall passes already printed, so do not order them too far ahead. Also, a prankster could ask for passes that last one second to overload the office.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA created two registries, ACME Order Auto-Renewal Fields and ACME Directory Metadata Auto-Renewal Fields, under a Specification Required policy. It added four ACME error types (autoRenewalCanceled, autoRenewalExpired, autoRenewalCancellationInvalid and autoRenewalRevocationNotSupported), the new Order fields auto-renewal and star-certificate, the directory metadata field auto-renewal, and the HTTP headers Cert-Not-Before and Cert-Not-After.
sections.eli5: The official lists got new entries for the new boxes, the new error messages and the two new date labels.
